title: The Encoder Equation
takeaway: This fixes what a "feature activation" concretely is in this paper: one non-negative number per dictionary element, produced by a single linear readout of the MLP activation vector followed by ReLU, computed after a learned offset has been subtracted from the input. Everything the paper later says about a feature firing, weakly or strongly, is a statement about this quantity.
walkthrough:
This is the encoder half of the paper's [[sparse-autoencoder]] — the rule that turns one activation vector into a list of [[feature]] activations.

The output $f_i(\mathbf{x})$ is the [[feature-activation]] of feature $i$ on datapoint $\mathbf{x}$. Here $\mathbf{x}$ is the MLP activation vector of the one-layer transformer being studied, a vector of 512 numbers ([[mlp-activations-as-target]]).

Read the operations in order. A fixed vector $\mathbf{b}_d$ is subtracted from the input. The matrix $W_e$ multiplies what is left. The vector $\mathbf{b}_e$ is added. ReLU clips anything negative to zero. The subscript $i$ then picks out the $i$-th entry of the resulting vector.

$W_e$ has one row per feature. Row $i$, dotted with the centred input, is a raw score for feature $i$ — large when the input points along that row's direction. So each row works as a detector. Having more rows than the input has dimensions is deliberate; the paper calls this [[overcompleteness]], and it follows from expecting the MLP to carry more features than neurons through [[superposition]].

$\mathbf{b}_e$ is an ordinary learned threshold. A negative entry means that feature needs a stronger match before it fires at all.

ReLU makes every activation zero or positive. A feature is therefore absent, or present with some intensity — it cannot fire negatively. Paired with the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]], which pushes most entries to exactly zero, this makes "did the feature fire here?" a plain yes-or-no question.

$\mathbf{b}_d$ is the [[pre-encoder-bias]], and its name comes from the decoder. The decoder reconstructs $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = W_d\mathbf{f} + \mathbf{b}_d$, adding back the same vector that was subtracted here; the paper ties the two rather than learning them separately. The effect is that the autoencoder fits the activations after a fixed offset is removed, so the [[feature-direction]]s stored in $W_d$ describe deviations from that offset instead of spending capacity on the offset itself.

Appendix 18.1 gives the reason it is there. On toy problems with a bias, the autoencoder failed to produce the expected [[bounce-plots]] unless a learned bias sat at both the encoder input and the decoder output. The bias is initialised to the geometric median of the activation dataset ([[geometric-median-initialization]]). The paper ranks this first among its architecture modifications, while saying plainly that it ran no rigorous ablations — the support offered is toy-model behaviour and intuition.

terms.definition: The activation of feature $i$ on datapoint $\mathbf{x}$: a single non-negative number saying how strongly that feature fires there. It is the $i$-th hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder.
The full vector of feature activations for one datapoint, of which $f_i$ is one entry. Its length equals the number of dictionary elements, not the number of neurons.
The input to the encoder: one datapoint's MLP activation vector from the transformer under study. This is the thing the paper is trying to decompose.
The centred input $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$, written explicitly in the appendix version of the same equation. It is what the encoder matrix actually multiplies.

The encoder weight matrix, with one row per feature and one column per input dimension. Each row is the detector for its feature; the dot product of that row with the centred input is the feature's raw score before bias and ReLU.
The pre-encoder bias, subtracted from the input before encoding and added back by the decoder on the way out. It is a single learned vector shared by both ends, not two independent biases.
The encoder bias, one learned number per feature, added to the raw scores before ReLU. A negative entry raises the bar the input must clear for that feature to fire.
The elementwise non-linearity applied last, replacing every negative entry with zero. Here its role is to make feature activations non-negative, so a feature is either off or on with some intensity.
An index selecting one coordinate of the vector the ReLU produced. It runs over the dictionary elements, so $i$ names a feature rather than a neuron.

The decoder weight matrix, named in the sentence following the equation. Its columns are the feature directions, and the same $\mathbf{b}_d$ that is subtracted here is added after multiplying by $W_d$.

The direction of feature $i$: the unit vector in activation space that feature $i$ writes along when it fires, equal to column $i$ of $W_d$. The encoder produces the coefficient, this is what the coefficient multiplies.
The input and output dimension of the autoencoder in the appendix notation, equal to the transformer's MLP width. $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}_d$ have $n$ entries.
The autoencoder's hidden width in the appendix notation: how many features the dictionary has. $W_e$ has $m$ rows and $\mathbf{b}_e$ has $m$ entries, with $m \geq n$.

numbers.meaning: The floor ReLU imposes on every feature activation. Any raw score that comes out negative becomes exactly zero, which is what makes a feature's state readable as absent versus present.
The MLP width of the one-layer transformer the paper studies, so the number of entries in $\mathbf{x}$, in $\mathbf{b}_d$, and in each row of $W_e$. Table 1 lists it as the transformer's MLP size.
The expansion factor the paper focuses on: eight times more dictionary features than neurons. With a 512-wide MLP that makes $W_e$ 4,096 rows tall, so 4,096 values of $f_i$ per datapoint.

The range of expansion factors across the paper's dictionary learning runs, from as many features as neurons up to 256 times as many. The same equation applies at every size; only the number of rows in $W_e$ changes.
The largest hidden width used, being 512 x 256. It is the upper end of how many $f_i$ values a single activation vector can be decomposed into here.

The number of MLP activation samples the autoencoder is trained on. $W_e$, $\mathbf{b}_e$ and $\mathbf{b}_d$ are all learned by gradient descent over this dataset, so it is what fixes the equation's numbers.

The L2 norm the columns of $W_d$ are constrained to. It matters for reading $f_i$ as an intensity: with directions pinned to unit length, the encoder cannot shrink a direction to inflate its activation, or vice versa.
